planting.note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before sowing in well-drained desert soil, and avoid rich amended beds that encourage weak, floppy growth.

directions: This fine-textured Australian shrub carries silvery, needle-like foliage made up of tiny cylindrical leaflets that give the whole plant a soft, feathery haze even in the harshest desert light. Clusters of bright yellow five-petaled flowers appear over an extended winter-into-spring bloom window, followed by flattened seed pods. It demands sharp drainage and minimal supplemental water once established, rotting quickly in heavy or frequently irrigated soil, and responds well to an occasional light shearing to keep its naturally loose, billowing form tidy. Use it as a low-water screen or background shrub in xeriscape and Mediterranean-climate gardens.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in consistently moist soil and prune hard each late winter to maximize the bright pink-and-white new growth that gives the cultivar its color.

directions: New spring shoots on this Japanese willow emerge a striking mottled pink, white, and green before settling into a cooler green-and-cream variegation through summer, making it one of the most colorful foliage shrubs for wet or streamside sites. Because the showiest coloring appears on fresh growth, an annual hard cutback in late winter or very early spring keeps plants compact and continuously colorful rather than letting them grow tall and leggy. It tolerates poorly drained soil better than almost any other variegated shrub and can also be trained as a small weeping standard. Give it steady moisture and full sun for the most vivid pink tones.

planting.note: Install as a grafted standard with the knuckle-like graft union well above soil level, and stake the thin trunk until it thickens enough to support the umbrella-shaped crown on its own.

directions: This male selection of goat willow is grafted at the top of a single straight trunk so its branches cascade straight down in a tight, umbrella-like dome, rather than arching outward like a full-size weeping willow. In late winter and earliest spring it is studded with plump, silvery-gray pussy willow catkins that turn bright yellow with pollen before the leaves emerge, making it a popular small specimen tree for tight urban and courtyard gardens. Because the whole canopy is a graft, any shoots arising from the straight trunk below the union should be removed promptly so they do not out-compete the weeping head. It adapts to average garden soil and does not need the constantly wet conditions many willows prefer.

planting.note: Push dormant hardwood cuttings directly into moist soil in early spring, or set rooted stock at the same depth it grew in the nursery pot, and shear annually to maintain its tidy rounded shape.

directions: A naturally compact, slow-growing selection of purple osier, this dwarf willow forms a neat rounded mound of slender blue-gray stems and narrow blue-green leaves without the suckering sprawl of the full-size species. It roots so readily from cuttings that gardeners commonly propagate replacements simply by pushing a dormant stem into damp ground. Its small size and fine texture make it useful as a low hedge, erosion-control planting on slopes, or informal border shrub where a full-sized willow would overwhelm the space. Occasional shearing in late winter keeps the habit dense and prevents the lower stems from thinning out.

planting.note: Site away from septic lines and paving since the fast, water-seeking roots can heave both, and stake young trees loosely as the twisted branch structure catches wind like a sail.

directions: Every twig, branch, and trunk of this willow grows in a tight spiral curl, giving even a leafless winter specimen striking sculptural interest and making its cut stems a favorite for flower arranging. It grows remarkably fast for a landscape tree but is relatively short-lived and brittle, regularly dropping small twigs and occasionally larger limbs in wind and ice storms, so it is best placed away from structures, walkways, and other prized plants. It thrives in consistently moist to wet soil along ponds and low areas and roots so easily from cut branches that volunteer seedlings and rooted twigs often appear nearby. Prune out damaged wood promptly to keep the twisting silhouette looking clean rather than ragged.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container nursery stock in deep, well-drained soil along streets or boulevards where a narrow crown and uniform shape are valued over spreading shade.

directions: This selection of littleleaf linden grows in a noticeably narrower, more upright oval than the species, making it a dependable choice for street tree plantings and tight urban sites where a wide-spreading canopy would conflict with sidewalks or utilities. Small, heart-shaped leaves cast dense but tidy shade, and in early summer the tree produces the same small, intensely fragrant creamy flowers typical of lindens, which draw bees from a considerable distance. It tolerates urban stresses such as compacted soil, heat, and pollution better than many shade trees, and its dense, uniform habit requires relatively little corrective pruning as it matures. Water regularly during the first few seasons to establish a deep root system before it is left to rely on natural rainfall.
